A Marian Story from the Heart of Africa

The reported apparitions at Kibeho, Rwanda, began on November 28, 1981, at a college in Kibeho. After years of investigation, the local Church formally recognised the apparitions in 2001, identifying Alphonsine Mumureke, Nathalie Mukamazimpaka and Marie Claire Mukangango as the three visionaries whose experiences were recognised.

The Church’s recognition described Mary as appearing under the title “Mother of the Word,” synonymous with Mother of God. It also stressed that the message associated with the apparitions does not constitute a new revelation, but recalls the ordinary teaching of the Church.

For anyone familiar with the name Kibeho but wanting to discover what actually happened there, The Apparitions of the Mother of the Word at Kibeho provides an opportunity to delve into this remarkable chapter of Marian history.

So, Where Do the Seven Sorrows Come In?

The connection becomes particularly significant through Marie Claire Mukangango, one of the recognised visionaries, who became associated with the Rosary of the Seven Sorrows of Mary.

The devotion invites Christians to contemplate the principal sorrows of Mary, including her suffering in connection with the life and Passion of Christ. Kibeho’s connection with this devotion is also reflected in the name of its Marian shrine: the Shrine of Our Lady of Sorrows.

In its 2001 declaration, the Diocese of Gikongoro described Kibeho as a place of prayer, conversion, reparation for sin and reconciliation, as well as a place that recalls the Gospel of the Cross.

This makes the Kibeho story especially fitting to revisit around the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows. It is not simply a story about an apparition; it opens a window into a spirituality centred on Mary’s sorrow, the Cross of Christ and the call to turn back to God.

A Message That Goes Beyond Kibeho

At the heart of the Kibeho message was a call to conversion, prayer and reconciliation. The Church’s recognition affirmed that the message associated with the apparitions was consistent with Sacred Scripture and the living tradition of the Church.

That gives the story an enduring relevance. Kibeho invites readers to reflect on how Christians respond to suffering, the need for conversion and the importance of prayer and reconciliation.
